english.html: law, which admonishes us not to deceive ourselves: for lechers and adulterers, says St Paul, shall not possess the kingdom of heaven h, and shall be judged by the living God i. Therefore, if some by misfortune had been so asleep until now as to connive at such crimes, it would be high time for them to awake from so deep a sleep, and, unsealing their eyes, to consider not so much what heretofore might have been done, whether here or elsewhere, as what is ordained and commanded us by God, or established by the civil laws k: especially when the adultery is aggravated, as in this case here, where the adultery is found qualified by a monstrous, and before this day unheard-of, treachery. One must not therefore doubt that the said du Tilh, by this crime alone, deserved death l: for, for a much lesser deed, a tavern servant, having abused his mistress, made drunk and asleep in the bed of her absent husband, was, by a decision of the Parlement of Paris pronounced in May 1551, hanged and strangled m. I do not know, however, whether from this penalty of death ordained against adulterers one could justly exempt, if not wholly (at least in part), priests, monks and others who by their own vow have voluntarily enslaved and bound themselves to perpetual continence. Which several have believed; for, they say, such kinds of people (to all of whom the Lord God has not dispensed the grace of being able to contain themselves), if they burn in such concupiscence, have no place where they may honestly satisfy their thirsty and carnal pleasure. Therefore, if they give themselves to some woman, even though she be married, they seem little or not at all to deserve some excuse [unclear: ſemblẽt peu, ou point meriter quelque excuſe; the argument being reported requires the opposite sense, that they deserve some excuse, and a word may have dropped] — like him who, constrained by hunger, steals a little food to appease it n. But this opinion is full of impiety, and the reason very cold: inasmuch as, in the first place, in things commanded or forbidden by the law of God, nay even by nature, simplicity, necessity or temptation does not excuse him who contravenes o. notes.original: La premiere des Corinthiens c. vi.
notes.gloss: Fornicators and adulterers shall not inherit the kingdom of God.
Whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.

notes.citation: Digest 1.18 (De officio praesidis), the fragment beginning Sed licet — not identified
notes.original: l. ſed licet. D. de offi. pre ſi.

notes.citation: Novels, Ut nulli iudicum (Nov. 134), chapter 10, § Si vero (the print says the sixth collatio; it is the ninth, as at {ſ} on p120); the authentica Sed hodie in Code 9.9
notes.original: P. ſi vero, vt null. iudi aux nouuelles ſouz la vi. col lation. Aut. ſed hodie de adult.
notes.gloss: Nov. 134.10 keeps the death penalty for the adulterer and changes it only for the woman.

notes.citation: Code 9.9 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis), the law beginning Quae adulterium (fragment not identified); Jean Papon, Recueil d'arrests notables des cours souveraines de France, title Des adulteres, arrêt 4
notes.original: l. que adul terium. C. de adult. Papon au titre des adulteres c. iiij.
notes.gloss: Papon reports the Parlement of Paris's decision of May 1551 hanging the tavern servant who abused his sleeping mistress.

notes.citation: Decretals, title De furtis (X 5.18), c. Si quis propter necessitatem (X 5.18.3)
notes.original: c. ſi quis propter. de furt.
notes.gloss: He who steals food from necessity of hunger does penance for three weeks: the lenient text the opinion Coras refutes relies on.

notes.citation: Code 2.2 (De in ius vocando), the law beginning Venia (fragment not identified); the Glossa ordinaria on the Decretum, Part III, De consecratione, D. 1, c. Sicut
notes.original: l. venia. C. de in ius voc. Gloſe au c. ſi-⟨alt:ſi.⟩ cut. de de cõſec. diſt. i.
notes.gloss: Necessity does not excuse what God's law forbids.

notes.citation: Digest 23.2 (De ritu nuptiarum), l. Palam, § Non est (D. 23.2.43.5, Ulpian)
notes.original: l. palam. P. non eſt. D. de ritu. nup.
notes.gloss: No pardon for the woman who has lived most shamefully under pretext of poverty — Coras's "poor woman who went astray to relieve her misery".
